hero.title: What does a dollar really cost?
hero.body: In much of the world the official exchange rate is not the rate anyone gets. This measures what people actually pay for a dollar — the kind an ordinary person can buy on their phone — in {count} currencies, every hour. Where there is no price, it says so, and why.

howItWorks.h1: Every number here links to the file it came from
howItWorks.sub: Tap any number to see how it was made.
subPoints: The official rate we compared against, and where it came from.
The sum that turns those two into the percentage you read.
The public data file, so you can redo the sum yourself.
howItWorks.subNote: No number is typed in by hand. When we miss an hour, the chart shows a gap. Every point you see was really collected.
howItWorks.dollarCostTitle: A dollar's price is the middle of real offers, every hour
howItWorks.dollarCostLead: Each country gets one price for a dollar every hour, built like this.
dollarCostPoints: A stablecoin is a coin that stays worth one US dollar.
We take the {minAds} cheapest offers to sell one on the exchange people there use. The middle offer is the price, so one odd seller cannot move it.
We set that price against the official rate at the same moment. The percentage is how much more a dollar really costs than that rate says.
A positive percentage means people pay more than the official rate. A negative one means they pay less.
With fewer than {minAds} sellers we publish no price. You see a gap, never a guess.
howItWorks.sendingCostTitle: Sending cost is the money lost against the mid-market rate
howItWorks.sendingCostLead: We price each app and the stablecoin route at {amounts} amounts, with the exchange fees and the fee for moving the coin counted. Look at the one closest to what you send.
howItWorks.sendingCostAmounts: The amounts are {amountList}, in the currency you send from.
sendingCostPoints: The mid-market rate is the middle price banks trade at with each other.
Whatever your recipient gets below that rate is what sending costs you.
howItWorks.notMeasuredTitle: Some costs are not in our figures, so check these yourself
notMeasured: The official rate updates only once a day. On days a currency moves fast, the gap we show can be a day behind.
Some exchanges do not publish what your bank charges to send money there, so we leave it out. Check your own bank's fee before you compare.
Some app prices are offers for a first transfer. If you have used that app before, you may pay more than we show.
We measure stablecoins only. If you are buying cash at a money changer, treat our numbers as a guide, not a quote.
howItWorks.sourcesTitle: Every price comes from a public source you can check
sourcesPoints: Dollar prices: Binance P2P, a marketplace where people trade with each other, {top}.
Official rates: open.er-api.com, frankfurter.app, Argentina's central bank.
App prices: {ownWord} apps quote us directly. The rest come from a public price comparison.

howItWorks.thresholdCounts: This hour {priced} currencies have a price and {notPriced} show a gap instead of a guess. A currency is priced when at least ten people are selling or an exchange gives a live price.

howItWorks.reactionCounts: We can test this in {qualified} of {total} countries. Each has at least {hours} hours of unbroken hourly prices.
howItWorks.reactionStep: We count an official rate move once it passes {threshold}%. The street price has caught up once it closes {closed}% of the gap that move opened. We look for that for up to {days} days.
howItWorks.reactionFindingLead: We guessed that where people pay most over the official rate, prices react slowest. Across every country we can test, the two are {relation}.
howItWorks.reactionRelationWeak: barely linked, with a score of {r} where zero means no link
howItWorks.reactionFindingBody: Algeria ({ccy}) has one of the widest gaps on the site, yet its prices react among the fastest. Turkey trades close to the official rate and reacts far slower. So a wide gap does not mean slow prices. See {countriesPage} for each country's own numbers.

howItWorks.askMethodTracked: Each hour we take the middle price from {evidence} ({source}). We set it against the official rate from the same check. The gap between them is the number. Nothing is estimated or smoothed.
howItWorks.askMethodGeneric: Each hour we take the middle of real offers and set it against the official rate. The gap is the number, never an estimate. With fewer than ten sellers, a country shows a reason instead. Every figure links to a file you can open.

machineRoom.title: Four AI agents run this site
machineRoom.lede: One collects the prices, one writes the code, one reviews it, one decides what to build next. The one that writes the code cannot approve it. One person sets the direction and holds the money and passwords, so no agent can spend money or change accounts. The site compares what it costs to send money from one country to another, so people can choose the cheapest way to send it.

roles.heading: Each agent has one job and cannot do the others'
roles.answer: The builder cannot merge its own work. The reviewer cannot write features. The planner never writes code.

items.text: Pulls prices from exchanges and money transfer providers and saves them to the data files.
Builds one task, then stops. If a task would break a rule, it refuses and says so.
Reads every change before it goes live and sends it back if it could make a price on the site wrong. It also recalculates a sample price from the saved files to confirm it still matches.
Decides what gets built next, and reports what happened. Never writes code, never merges.

tape.title: What people pay for a dollar, updating every {minutes} minutes
tape.lede: Each row shows what people pay, the official rate, and the difference. Prices are in each country's own currency per US dollar, marked by its three letter code, such as AFN for the Afghan afghani. Central Africa and West Africa are groups of countries that share one currency. The difference is how much more people pay than the official rate, as a percentage. A minus sign means they pay less.
tape.statusIdleLate: The last check is older than {minutes} minutes. This is not a fault. A check may be running or late. The prices shown are from the last check, at the time above.
tape.statusLive: Connected. New prices appear here as each check finishes.
tape.statusOffline: Not connected, so prices may be out of date. Next check at {time} UTC.
tape.statusOfflineLate: Not connected. The last check is older than {minutes} minutes. A check may be running or late. The prices shown are from the last check, at the time above. Reload to try again.
tape.metaTemplate: Last checked on {date} at {time} UTC. {n} countries priced.
tape.unavailable: The latest prices could not be loaded. Try again in a few minutes.
tape.note: A stablecoin is a digital token built to hold the value of a US dollar. What people pay comes from offers on Binance, a large online marketplace where people trade stablecoins. We line up the offers to sell a digital dollar from lowest to highest and take the one in the middle, so a few odd offers do not move the price. We compare it with the official rate, which is the bank exchange rate at the same moment. Stablecoins can be swapped for cash dollars at close to one for one, so their price is a good guide to what a dollar costs on the street. Cash prices can differ a little. If people pay more than the official rate, a dollar is hard to get at the bank price.
tape.linkText: See each country's price over time →
tape.footer: The first two numbers in each row come from the latest check. The difference is worked out from those two.

Prices come from offers to sell stablecoins, digital tokens worth one dollar, on markets where people trade directly with each other. countries.pegTitle: Currencies fixed to the dollar or euro
countries.pegNote: These currencies hold their official rate, so paying more is the cost of getting hold of a digital dollar, not a currency losing value. A digital dollar is a stablecoin, a token meant to stay worth one dollar. Fixed means the government holds its currency at a set rate. Here that means the CFA franc, one currency shared by several countries in Africa, fixed to the euro. It also means the Gulf currencies, each fixed to the dollar.
countries.nearTitleTemplate: {n} {countries} where people pay the official rate, give or take {gap}%
countries.nearNote: A plus sign means people pay more than the official rate and a minus sign means less.
countries.withheldNoteTemplate: We only publish a price when at least {min} people are selling. Fewer than that is not a market, so we say so instead of guessing.
countries.cfaNote: Each CFA entry is a currency shared by several countries. We count it once, as one price.
countries.depthNoteTemplate: "How much you could buy" is how many dollars are on offer near that price. A price with almost no money behind it is not really a price. A plus sign means at least that much, because we stop counting there. A gap is how much more people pay than the official rate. The small figure under each Gap now is how much that gap moved since the Gap on date, in percentage points. A note beside a country code says why that price is less certain. Buy and sell prices far apart means sellers ask much more than buyers offer, so we still show the price but trust it less.

findingData.indexHeading: When and how much you send changes the cost
findingData.indexLine: Each finding is worked out from prices we store every hour. Each page shows the evidence, how it was worked out, and a file you can download.
findingData.methodHeading: This is how we built it
findingData.methodFilesLabel: The code that works it out, open for anyone to read:
findingData.limitsHeading: Read the number with these limits
findingData.downloadNote: The file lists every row behind the number, one line per hour or per price change. The table above summarises them.
findingData.notFound: We have no published finding at this address.
findingData.unit_price_changes: confirmed price changes by transfer apps since our record began
findingData.unit_weekend_increases: Saturday price rises that came back down by the Tuesday after
findingData.unit_sgd_per_month: Singapore dollars sent per month in total. Above it, stablecoins cost less for a transfer of five thousand to the Philippines.
findingData.title_price_changes: Transfer apps keep changing their prices
findingData.claim_price_changes: Transfer apps raise and cut what they charge to send money. The cheapest app when you compare may not be the cheapest when you send.
findingData.evidenceBasis_price_changes: Each row is one route: its confirmed changes, how many were rises or cuts, and how many apps moved.
findingData.method_price_changes: We record each app's cost every hour, for each amount sent, against the real exchange rate. A change counts only when one app's daily cost moved against every other app on the same route. It must move the same way, on the same day, by more than a small set amount. Moves that every app shares come from the exchange rate and never count. Each day needs several hourly readings, and a day is judged only once it has ended.
findingData.limits_price_changes: Each amount sent counts on its own. An app that changes its price at several amounts counts once for each. The number does not say how big any change was. It covers only the routes and apps we check, from the day each was added.
findingData.title_weekend_penalty: Some apps charge more on Saturday, then cut back
findingData.claim_weekend_penalty: A rise counts when an app charged more on a Saturday and came back down by Tuesday. If your transfer can wait, a weekday can cost less.
findingData.evidenceBasis_weekend_penalty: Each row is one route: its Saturday rises that came back, the cuts that undid them, and how many Saturdays we checked.
findingData.method_weekend_penalty: We start from the confirmed price changes. A rise counts when an app raised its price on a Saturday. The same app must then cut its price on the same route by the Tuesday after. Both moves must be in our data. We never assume a return from the rise alone.
findingData.limits_weekend_penalty: Each amount sent counts on its own. One Saturday rise counts once for each amount it showed up at. The number does not say how much more a Saturday cost. A route with few Saturdays checked has had little chance to show this.
findingData.title_volume_crossover: Stablecoins beat the cheapest app only above about {approx} a month, a figure worked out from the exchanges' published fee tiers
findingData.claim_volume_crossover: Sending five thousand Singapore dollars to the Philippines, a stablecoin would beat the cheapest app only above this monthly volume. Nobody in our data traded that much, and we never saw it happen: the figure is rebuilt from the exchanges' fee tiers. A stablecoin is a coin that stays worth one US dollar.
findingData.evidenceBasis_volume_crossover: Both rows are the same transfer, priced for two ways of buying on the exchange. Costs are in hundredths of a percent.
findingData.method_volume_crossover: We take every real check of sending five thousand Singapore dollars to the Philippines by stablecoin. For a given monthly volume, we look up the lower fee each exchange would charge. We rebuild each check's cost with those fees, from its own recorded prices. The number is the lowest volume where its usual cost drops below the cheapest app's usual cost. Both come from the same hours.
findingData.limits_volume_crossover: It covers one route and one amount. The number is rebuilt from real prices, never seen happening. Nobody in our data traded at that volume. It does not mean stablecoins are cheaper for most senders. Below that volume, the cheapest app costs less for this transfer.
findingData.limits_sgd_php_never_cheapest: It covers one route and only the hours we priced. It does not say a stablecoin can never win: on other routes it was the cheapest in some hours, and this route may change.
findingData.method_sgd_php_never_cheapest: Every hour we price a stablecoin path and each app for this route. A stablecoin counts as cheapest when its cost is below every app's cost in that hour. The count is the same one the home page and the routes page print.
findingData.evidenceBasis_sgd_php_never_cheapest: Each row is one amount sent from Singapore to the Philippines: the hours we priced, and the hours in which a stablecoin was cheapest.
findingData.unit_hours_stablecoin_cheapest: hours in which a stablecoin was the cheapest way to send
findingData.claim_sgd_php_never_cheapest: In no hour we priced did a stablecoin beat the cheapest app, at any of the five amounts. A stablecoin is a coin that stays worth one US dollar.
findingData.title_sgd_php_never_cheapest: Singapore to the Philippines: a stablecoin was never the cheapest way to send
